opus-5.5.text:
I think about this a lot, actually. When you're young, especially if you grew up in a fairly competitive environment, the external standards are very clear. There's an exam, there's a ranking, there's a competition, and you know exactly what "good" looks like. That clarity is comfortable, and to be honest it's useful for a while. It gives you structure and it forces you to build basic skills.

But at some point I started to feel that the standards of a small circle can quietly become your whole definition of success. In academia, for example, there's a community that cares about certain kinds of problems, certain kinds of papers, certain kinds of elegance. If you only optimize for what that circle values, you can do very well inside it and still end up working on things that don't matter much outside it. You're climbing a hill without asking whether it's the right hill.

So my view now is that external standards are a tool, not a goal. They tell you something real. If smart people in a field think your work is weak, you should take that seriously. But they're also lagging indicators. They reflect what people already understand to be important. If you want to do something new, almost by definition the existing evaluation system won't fully recognize it at first.

What I try to do is keep two questions separate. First, am I actually good at this, by a standard I'd defend to myself? Second, does the world currently reward it? The first one I care about a lot. The second one I care about less than I used to. When those diverge, I try to trust my own judgment about what's interesting and important, while staying humble enough to check whether I'm just fooling myself.

And I think there's a kind of freedom in that. Once you stop needing the approval of a particular circle, you can move between fields, change directions, and work on problems because they're genuinely exciting rather than because they'll look good on a CV. That's been the most valuable shift for me.

r002.rationale: It says clear standards provide structure and help build skills, but does not claim that doing well is easy once the criteria are known.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I try not to let either of them become the thing that drives me, but I also don't pretend they don't matter.

External standards, like publication counts, citations, which lab you're at, which company hired you, are useful as rough signals. They tell you something about whether your work is landing. But they're lagging indicators, and they're noisy. If you optimize for them directly, you end up doing the kind of work that is legible to a committee rather than the kind of work that actually moves things. A lot of the ideas I'm most happy about, like the early agent work, looked a bit strange when I started. If I had been checking them against what a review cycle wanted, I probably wouldn't have pursued them.

The small circle thing is more subtle. When you're in a tight community, say a handful of people working on language agents or on reasoning, the group develops its own taste, its own sense of what's cool and what's not. That taste is often much better than the external metric, because these are people who actually understand the problem. So I do care what they think. If someone whose judgment I respect tells me an idea is boring, I take that seriously.

But the danger is that a small circle can also become an echo chamber. Everyone agrees on the same framing, the same benchmarks, the same definition of progress, and then the whole group can be wrong together. I've seen that happen. So I try to hold it as one input, not as the ground truth.

What I actually come back to is a kind of internal question: do I believe this matters, and would I still think so if nobody was watching? If the answer is yes, then external standards and the circle's opinion are things to learn from, not things to satisfy. If the answer is no, then no amount of recognition is going to make the work feel worth it.

And practically, I think the way you earn the freedom to ignore standards is by meeting them first, at least a little. You need enough credibility that people will give your weird idea a chance. So it's not really a choice between the two. It's more like you pay the entry fee, and then you spend the rest of your time trying to work on what you actually think is right.

r001.rationale: The response discusses external standards and a small circle’s opinions as signals, but does not compare meeting them to training a model.

r002.rationale: The response does not claim that meeting a small circle’s standards is easy once its criteria are known; it describes those standards as useful but potentially echo-chamber prone.

astra-6.text:
I think external standards are useful as feedback, but they become limiting when you treat them as the goal. A small circle can have very clear criteria for what counts as good work, and you can become very good at satisfying those criteria without asking whether the work matters outside that circle.

Of course, you can’t simply say, “I don’t care what anyone thinks.” You need to learn from other people and understand why those standards exist. But you also need to gradually develop your own judgment: What problem do I think is important? What would convince me that I’ve made progress? Would I still want to do this if it didn’t get recognition from the people around me?

For me, the useful distinction is between understanding a standard and letting it decide your direction. You can take feedback seriously while still choosing a different direction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think external standards can be useful feedback, but they shouldn’t become the goal itself. A small circle often has a shared sense of what counts as good work, and learning those standards can help you improve. But if you only optimize for their approval, you can gradually lose sight of why the work matters to you.

I’d try to separate two questions: What can I learn from this evaluation? And is this actually the thing I want to optimize for? You can take criticism seriously without accepting someone else’s entire definition of success. The difficult part is developing your own judgment while keeping it open to correction.
